April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
WOW - Thank you! It was wonderful to see our Instant Gallery tables overflow last month - literally. It
is not an understatement to say that showing your
work, regardless of your ability or your experience,
that your peers really do want to see what you are
making. Please don't be shy - bring in something!
The Guild has begun discussions with several world
class demonstrators for visiting us for a traditional
all day demo and followed up with classes. In the
mix are Graeme Priddle and Melissa Engler, Kirk De
Heer, Mike Hosaluk, and Yann Morot. At press time,
Tom Wirsing is booked to be our first visiting demonstrator and will be here in early September. If
you are unfamiliar with any of these fine people,
they are easy to find via your favourite WWW
search engine.
With a little luck, before you renew your membership in the Fall, we will have integrated a payment
system on the membership form. It’s currently being tested by the IT Team. Also being evaluated is a
members’ only zone where things like our proprietary videos can be accessed.
Our last public exhibition was in 2019 at The Port
Moody Arts Centre. We have initiated the process
to hold another exhibit at pomoarts.ca With this in
mind I encourage any of you to explore other opportunities for us to show the public what we make
and (sometimes when possible) how we make it.
Speaking of Port Moody, they are also running their
“Arts Shuffle” on June 14 and we are going to be
there! It’s an informal opportunity for us to show
our work and how we make it. Everyone is welcome to show something. Bruce Campbell is coordinator for the event.
FLEA MARKET! June 15 at Sapperton Hall. Anyone
with the Guild is welcome to donate, sell on their
own behalf, barter, or haggle to your heart’s content. There will be a silent auction with several really nice tools, various accessories such as chucks, as
well as a small lathe. You are also welcome to donate to the auction if you wish. This is an excellent
opportunity for you to clear out and make space so
that you can…wait for it, buy more tools! There is
no cover charge. The auction list will be mailed out
closer to the big date. Out of towners wishing to
partake can use a proxy to bid on your behalf… just
so you do not feel left out.
The Guild submitted an entry for the The AAW
Communications Excellence Award. To see what
we submitted click here.
GVWG Board meetings are always open to members for you to listen in. They are always via Zoom
and traditionally occur every other month. The next
one is May 13. To get invited send the President a
note.
The President’s Challenge for May is Spinning Top.
Steve

April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
A big Thank You to all those who have contributed
articles for both this issue and in the past. This
month, Brian tells us the story of his piece featured
on the cover of this month’s newsletter and our
webmaster reveals some interesting statistics on
who is looking at our website and what they're
looking at.
Claire has provided an announcement and information about the upcoming Sculptor’s Society Exhibition in May. This show will likely be of interest to
many of our members.
This month’s featured Member Profile is of yours
truly (Diana made me do it). While we are a bit
light on editorial this month, we make up for it
with a good-sized gallery of some wonderful turnings from last month’s meeting. As always, please
consider contributing articles, tips, etc. We may
look like a little e-magazine, but we don’t have a
staff of writers; just me and I’m not all that interesting.
Steve
After spending hours and hours editing our newsletter last month Steve Fairbairn asked me to check
the statistics on how many people download our
Newsletter. Was all of his time and effort worthwhile? Did we have readership? As it turns out our
latest NL was downloaded 174 times in March. Previous months are similar. There’s no way to determine who downloaded but it is safe to say our
members make up a large portion of that, and with
good reason? With great articles like our Member
Profiles, Safety tips, Tech/Talk summaries, interesting articles on techniques, cover page featured,
and so on - we have an excellent publication!
Thank You Steve! And thank you to those that provide the quality content.
Here are some other selected stats from March:
We average about 900 unique visitors/month from
45 countries. These are users that actually opened
one of our pages or files. My favourite is a loan visitor in Seychelles – 1000Km from Mogadishu and
800 Km from Madagascar… I wonder what they
found on our site?

Occasionally either Ed Pretty, who fields our info@gvwg.ca emails, or president@gvwg.ca receive
feedback from people that found good use from
something on our site or newsletter – that is nice
to see.
As a side note, an astonishing number of wood
turning clubs hide their NL from public access. Also,
I have not seen another wood turning website that
has a gallimaufry page. Remember this, the newsletter and the website are your newsletter and
your website. Please consider contributing something. For the website, take a look at our resources
page and ask yourself if you have something to
share.

I first made this vase in May 2023 and called it “Le
Ver” (The Worm) because it was shaped using
French Curves and was riddled with worm holes.
Using old dentist pick tools, I
removed the massive amount
of worm dust out of every single hole, inside and out. Thinking it was done, I would give it
a tap and find more dust.
There was the odd dried up
old worm in there and the
thought never left me that this
dust “passed” through
that worm.
I
used
inspiration
from woodturners like
Art Liestman to concentrate
on
the
shape. So I used my
home made Fibonacci
gauge to mark out where the French Curves would
start and end. The black is India Ink with an airbrush silver pearlescent highlight.
After displaying in our house
for a few months I realized unless the vase was in good sunlight, the worm holes were not
very visible.
Along came Pres. Steve’s Challenge, “Before and After”. Time
to relook at this vase.
I painted inside every worm
hole with FW Pearlescent Liquid Acrylic Sun-Up
Blue from Opus Art Supply. Took 3 coats because
of the strong black background
and the undulated surfaces inside the holes. Once the holes
were redone I touched up the
India Ink with a teardrop foam
makeup applicator, a trick I
learned
from
another
woodturner from San Diego, Joe
Flemming. I made sure that the
girls in the Sally Beauty Store
knew I was using these for woodturning.
I am now happy with how the light works with this
vase.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
I would like to invite the GVWG Guild members to
the Sculptor’s Society of BC 50th Anniversary Exhibition (1974 -2024) at the Pendulum Art Gallery
Vancouver BC, May 13 – June 8, 2024. On display
will be the woodturning results from my Guild participation starting in 2019.
When I joined the GVWG I loved meeting everyone
and enrolled in the” Turning 101” at KMS. I struggled to turn bowls like most people who are new,
but really wanted to continue wood turning as a
part of my sculpture practice. Keith Ruttan invited
me to his shop where 3 or four of us met regularly
on Wednesday’s. I had ambitions to turn plexiglass
and brass along with wood and Keith and the dear
late Barry Wilkinson rose to the challenge! I am
forever grateful for their generous support and education.
The February 2020 GVWG newsletter shows my
first wood turning project titled “Light Motif”. I
was mentored by many of you in the GVWG, but
most significantly Keith and Barry. Thank you to all!
Meanwhile 4 years later….I am excited to share
that I have completed 5 turned, multimedia works.
They will be exhibited at the Pendulum Art Gallery,
May 13 – June 8, 2024 as part of this a group exhibition of the B C Sculptors’ Society. I have been a
member with the Sculptor’s Society since 2003.
I am sure that I am the first Sculptors’ Society of BC
member to show wood turning in a SSBC show.
I invite you to come and meet the Sculptors, where
all guilds can connect and share ideas!
Opening Reception is Saturday, May 18 2024
2:00pm - 4:00pm.
The exhibition is open May 13 - June 8, 2024.
Address: Pendulum Gallery, 885 West Georgia St.,
Vancouver BC.
Barry Wilkinson
Keith Ruttan

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I started woodturning in 2001 when I inherited an
old Rockwell Beaver lathe and Craftsman tools
from my father after he passed away. I had already
been an avid flat woodworker for a few years.
While trying to teach myself to turn wood, I quickly
became dissatisfied with the lathe and, during the
annual woodworking show in Cloverdale, I purchased a Canwood (House of Tools) lathe which I
used for a couple of years. At the same time, I
signed up for a night school woodturning class
taught by Scott Belway. I learned a lot during that
course and it really kickstarted me into making progress as a turner. During those lessons, I discovered the GVWG and was able to sign up for a weekend workshop taught by Stuart Batty. That was life
changing for me and resulting in me setting aside
all my flat woodworking endeavors and focus on
woodturning for the next couple of years. It was
during that time that I upgraded to a Nova 3000
lathe with a motor controller. That was a huge
step up in technology and capabilities and I used
that lathe for over 15 years before acquiring a wellused, but well maintained, Oneway 2436 which is
the lathe I use today.
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
My current workshop is a 22x24 sq. ft. double garage that I purpose built as a workshop when I
bought my current home in 2005. It is well stocked
with woodworking/woodturning tools and equipment as well as a metal lathe and milling machine.
My wood-storage shed collapsed in a snowstorm
about 10 years ago which necessitated the move of
my coveted wood collection into the workshop,
taking up a lot of valuable space. Sadly, my wood
hoard remains in my workshop making for a
crowded, but still very usable, workspace. You can
take a quick tour of my workshop by watching this
YouTube video I recorded for the club’s August
2021 Virtual Shop Crawl. The shop hasn’t changed
much since then.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
I can’t say I have any favourite tools. I grew up
with my father’s wisdom that you should “always
use the correct tool for the job. If you don’t have
the correct tool, get one. If you can’t get one,
make one.” The tool I like using the most is what I
consider to be the “right tool” for the operation I
am currently performing.
(Continued on page 9)
Woodturning corner of workshop

April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
What is your favourite wood?
I love turning hard, exotic woods but I’m also
cheap so I’m generally limited to domestic hardwoods. The wood I turn most is Big Leaf Maple because it is cheap (or free), readily available and can
have amazing figure.
What finishes do you prefer using?
I don’t have a favourite finish. My choice of finish
is dependent on the project and what it will be
used for. I prefer simple finishes that are easy to
apply such as wipe-on poly and various oil finishes.
I’ve been experimenting lately with embellishment
techniques and have been using a variety of airbrush pigments. Other than rattle cans, I have yet
to venture into spray finishes, but it is high on my
list of techniques to try.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
I don’t generally combine other materials into my
projects unless you count peppermill and pen
mechanisms. I’m not opposed to other materials; I
just haven’t ventured there yet.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
I enjoy flat woodworking, both hand and machine,
and have taught introductory evening classes as
well as pre-apprenticeship classes for a non-profit
on Vancouver’s Downtown East Side. I have a side
gig doing custom laser cutting and engraving. I like
to experiment with ways to incorporate laser technology into some of my projects.
I spent much of my early career as an electronics/
computer technician and still have an interest in
electronics.
Prior to taking up woodworking, I was heavily into
stained glass. Every 6- or 7-years l drag my stained
-glass stuff out and build a panel or two.
During the pandemic I rekindled an old passion for
photography that I had during my teens and 20’s
with a particular interest in bird photography.
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
Most of my ideas come from GVWG demos and
weekend workshops as well as other woodturners’
projects that I find intriguing or inspiring. I get a lot
of inspiration from our own member galleries but
also from a few online sources. I rarely have an
original idea of my own.
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
I would have to say my greatest maker influences
(Continued from page 8)
(Continued on page 10)
Camo Platter
Saturn vessel - laser engraved

April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
were my parents. My mother is a lifelong artist
and seamstress, even now at 95. My father was an
aircraft mechanic, musician and jack of all trades.
Both were the epitome of makers and shared the
philosophy that I seem to have inherited:
“Anything worth doing is worth overdoing”. Both
were children of The Great Depression and instilled
in me the philosophy of “waste not, want not” and
that repairing is preferable to replacing. That
would explain my scrap wood hoard and my inability to get rid of old tools, books, etc.
In terms of woodturning, I would say that my
greatest influences are the demonstrating turners
at the GVWG. I’ve never been to a demo or workshop where I didn’t learn something new and was
inspired to experiment with or improve a particular
skill.
Where do you usually display and/or sell your
work?
Other than the GVWG Instant Gallery or President’s Challenge, I don’t publicly display my work. Most of my work that I’m happy with is given away
and the rest becomes part of my “personal collection”. I don’t sell my work although I have taken
on the odd commission.
What is the most challenging piece that you
have made so far?
My most challenging projects have been deep, hollow vessels. I enjoy the adrenaline rush of getting
close to the bottom or target wall thickness knowing that a slight error of judgement or technique on
my part can cause the piece to explode.
What is your favorite project to date?
I can’t say I have any one favourite project in particular. If I just feel like turning and having nothing
in mind, I usually end up with a small hollow vessel
or lidded cup. Lately, I lean toward wide-rimmed
platters that become canvases for embellishment
experiments.
Where do you see your work going in the future?
(Continued from page 9)
(Continued on page 11)
Hollow Vessel - Maple & Padauk, 4” tall
Lidded Cup - Maple Burl & Padauk., 5” tall

April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
I watched a recent demonstration by Art Liestman
where he categorized woodturning as either
(paraphrasing) artistic or sport turning. I fall
squarely into the sport turning category. In my
case, Woodturning ADD. I see a particular form or
technique that intrigues me, and I experiment to
the point where I feel I have “figured it out”. I likely haven’t mastered it, but I’ve satisfied the curiosity, scratched it itch, and then go on to the next
thing. Of course, this is contrary to just about everything we are taught about perfecting a skillset or
developing our own unique style. So, where I see
my work going in the future, is whatever intrigues
me or piques my curiosity at the time.
Are there any new techniques you would like
to try?
Yes, everything I haven’t yet tried.

Cathy Friesen - Pin Cushion from Candlestick Holder
Palo Santo
My father-in-law had made some candlestick holders
from Palo Santo and then epoxied them.
I removed the screw but when I turned off the epoxy the
wood was no longer the rich dark brown colour but back
to the green wood.
Even though the turning was many years old, once the
epoxy was removed the oils in the wood began to leech
out again.
I buffed it several times with diamond compound on the
Beall Buffing system before it stopped shedding oil.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 33)

April 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 33
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
